headline: One Photo of a Mountain Lion Changed Conservation Forever
meta_description: A photojournalist's iconic image of mountain lion P-22 sparked a movement that led to the world's largest wildlife crossing opening in Los Angeles.
summary_short: Steve Winter's year-long quest to photograph a mountain lion against the Hollywood sign sparked a conservation movement that inspired funding for a groundbreaking wildli…
body:
Photographer Steve Winter spent fifteen months waiting in the dark hills of Griffith Park to capture a single image: a mountain lion named P-22, collar glinting, padding down a hillside with the Hollywood sign luminous in the distance. When a National Park Service biologist insisted there were no mountain lions in the park, Winter knew better. That photograph, when it finally came, became more than a technical triumph—it became a turning point for conservation in Los Angeles. The image helped spark a movement that eventually inspired funding for the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing over U.S. Route 101, which will be the world's largest wildlife crossing when it opens on December 2.

This transformation from a single photograph into real-world conservation impact is the heart of a new book called Big Cats, created by Winter and Mongabay contributing editor Sharon Guynup. The nine stories in the book were selected specifically because each one produced tangible results. Winter spent months in the Himalayan cold to photograph snow leopards and deliver vaccines to farmers in the Zankar Valley, reducing retaliatory killings of the big cats. Guynup and Winter went undercover at a Buddhist temple in Thailand, exposing a three-million-dollar tourism operation that was actually a front for tiger trafficking—leading to its shutdown by the Thai authorities.

The deeper lesson is elegantly simple. As Guynup explains it: storytelling and photography can change the world. When people see the real faces of endangered species and understand the ecosystems that depend on them, they act. The book, released October 6, stands as evidence that science combined with compelling communication can inspire communities to protect the environment, one frame at a time.
quick_facts: P-22 mountain lion photo took 15 months to capture in Griffith Park, Los Angeles
Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing opens December 2 as world's largest wildlife overpass
Tiger Temple investigation exposed $3 million trafficking operation in Thailand
Book features nine conservation stories with proven real-world impact
Steve Winter photographed snow leopards in Zankar Valley, Himalayas
